title: Eliminating the Parameter
short: Solve for t or use an identity to get one equation in x and y.

blocks.html: Parametric equations are great for motion, but to recognize the shape of the path it helps to have one equation in $x$ and $y$. Removing $t$ is called eliminating the parameter.

Either solve one equation for $t$ and substitute into the other, or find an identity that links the two, such as $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$ or $\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t = 1$. Then check which $x$- and $y$-values the original equations can actually reach.

Every point on the path satisfies both equations for the same $t$. If $t$ can be written in terms of $x$, putting that into the $y$-equation gives a relation that every point of the path satisfies. With trig functions, the Pythagorean identity plays the same role without solving for $t$.

blocks.name: pre-param
blocks.cap: This path is the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{9} + \frac{y^2}{4} = 1$. The single equation shows the shape; the parametric form also shows the motion.

blocks.title: Use an identity
steps: Isolate the trig functions: $\cos t = \frac{x}{3}$ and $\sin t = \frac{y}{2}$.

blocks.title: Watch the restrictions
steps: But $x = \sqrt{t}$ is never negative, so only the right half of that parabola is traced.

blocks.html: Forgetting the restrictions. For $x = t^2$, $y = t^4$ you get $y = x^2$, but $x = t^2$ can never be negative, so the path is only the right half of the parabola. Check the range of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ before you sketch.
